async function withWorkerFileLock<T>(
  runId: string,
  workerId: string,
  task: (paths: WorkerStreamPaths) => Promise<T>,
): Promise<T> {
  const paths = await workerStreamPaths(runId, workerId, "write");
  await fs.mkdir(path.dirname(paths.filePath), { recursive: true });
  // Appending an empty string with `a` is an atomic touch.
  await fs.writeFile(paths.filePath, "", { flag: "a" });
  const release = await acquireWorkerFileLock(paths.lockPath);
  try {
    return await task(paths);
  } finally {
    await release();
  }
}

async function readWorkerFileState(runId: string, workerId: string) {
  const paths = await workerStreamPaths(runId, workerId, "read");
  try {
    const stat = await fs.stat(paths.filePath);
    return { size: stat.size, mtimeMs: stat.mtimeMs };
  } catch (error) {
    if ((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "ENOENT") {
      return { size: 0, mtimeMs: 0 };
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

// per-request latency budget. Write-mode resolution runs through
// ensureArtifactStreamRow, which itself caches downstream; we still
// memoize here so the cache key matches across read/write.
const workerStreamPathsCache = new Map<string, WorkerStreamPaths>();

// Tracks worker chains whose `artifact_streams` row has been ensured
// for write in this process. A separate set from `workerStreamPathsCache`
// because the path cache is populated by both read- and write-mode
// resolution — and read-mode resolution does NOT create the row. So if
// the first call for a chain was a read, the path got cached but no row
// was ever inserted; later write calls used to hit the path cache,
// skip `ensureArtifactStreamRow`, and append to disk forever without a
// metadata row. Result: hand-repairs every time a worker is spawned
// after a cancel (see worker-3 in run 2182b07381c8). Tracking
// ensure-for-write separately lets us populate the row exactly once
// per chain per process, even if a read warmed the path cache first.
const ensuredForWriteByKey = new Set<string>();

async function workerStreamPaths(
  runId: string,
  workerId: string,
  mode: "read" | "write",
): Promise<WorkerStreamPaths> {
  const key = chainKey(runId, workerId);
  if (mode === "write" && !ensuredForWriteByKey.has(key)) {
    try {
      const { ensureArtifactStreamRow } = await import("@/server/artifacts/stream-metadata");
      const row = await ensureArtifactStreamRow({
        runId,
        kind: "worker_entries",
        ownerId: workerId,
      });
      const resolved: WorkerStreamPaths = {
        filePath: row.location.filePath,
        compressedFilePath: row.location.compressedFilePath,
        lockPath: row.location.lockPath,
      };
      workerStreamPathsCache.set(key, resolved);
      ensuredForWriteByKey.add(key);
      return resolved;
    } catch (error) {
      if (String((error as Error).message ?? "").includes("missing run")) {
        const resolved = legacyWorkerStreamPaths(runId, workerId);
        workerStreamPathsCache.set(key, resolved);
        ensuredForWriteByKey.add(key);
        return resolved;
      }
      throw error;
    }
  }

  const cached = workerStreamPathsCache.get(key);
  if (cached) return cached;

  const legacyPaths = legacyWorkerStreamPaths(runId, workerId);
  if (existsSync(legacyPaths.filePath) || existsSync(legacyPaths.compressedFilePath)) {
    workerStreamPathsCache.set(key, legacyPaths);
    return legacyPaths;
  }

  // Read-mode cold path. We do NOT insert an artifact_streams row here
  // — that's exclusively a write responsibility.
  let resolved: WorkerStreamPaths;
  const [{ db }, { runs }] = await Promise.all([
    import("@/server/db"),
    import("@/server/db/schema"),
  ]);
  const run = await db
    .select({ projectPath: runs.projectPath })
    .from(runs)
    .where(eq(runs.id, runId))
    .get();
  if (!run) {
    resolved = legacyWorkerStreamPaths(runId, workerId);
  } else {
    const location = await resolveArtifactStreamLocation(
      {
        runId,
        kind: "worker_entries",
        ownerId: workerId,
        projectPath: run.projectPath ?? null,
      },
      "read",
    );
    resolved = {
      filePath: location.filePath,
      compressedFilePath: location.compressedFilePath,
      lockPath: location.lockPath,
    };
  }
  workerStreamPathsCache.set(key, resolved);
  return resolved;
}

#!/usr/bin/env tsx
import { db } from "@/server/db";
import { workers } from "@/server/db/schema";
import { and, eq, ne } from "drizzle-orm";
import {
  parseLegacyOutputEntriesJson,
  writeWorkerOutputEntries,
} from "@/server/workers/output-store";

async function main() {
  const rows = await db
    .select({
      id: workers.id,
      runId: workers.runId,
      outputEntriesJson: workers.outputEntriesJson,
    })
    .from(workers)
    .where(and(ne(workers.outputEntriesJson, ""), ne(workers.outputEntriesJson, "[]")));

  console.log(`Found ${rows.length} workers with persisted output entries.`);
  let migrated = 0;
  let skipped = 0;

  for (const row of rows) {
    const entries = parseLegacyOutputEntriesJson(row.outputEntriesJson);
    if (entries.length === 0) {
      skipped += 1;
      continue;
    }
    await writeWorkerOutputEntries(row.runId, row.id, entries);
    await db.update(workers).set({ outputEntriesJson: "" }).where(eq(workers.id, row.id));
    migrated += 1;
  }

  console.log(`Migrated ${migrated} workers (skipped ${skipped}).`);
}

main().then(() => process.exit(0)).catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exit(1);
});

  runId: string,

  if (!Array.isArray(entries) || entries.length === 0) {
    return;
  }

  await runOnChain(runId, workerId, async () => {
    await withWorkerFileLock(runId, workerId, async (paths) => {
      await expandWorkerOutputFileInternal(paths);

      const { fingerprints } = await refreshChainCaches(runId, workerId);

## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T20:46:53.791Z

So the deduplication in `writeWorkerOutputEntries` works by matching against the `(id, fingerprint)` pairs from `refreshChainCaches`, and sequences are assigned from the cursor. The real issue is that during those three live runs, both the migration process and the server process were executing `withWorkerFileLock` simultaneously—they're competing for the same filesystem lock.

The server's in-memory cache is keyed by file size and mtime, and `nextSeqByKey` lives in memory too. The server's cursor started at 1399 based on `dbLatestSeq`. The migration wrote entries 1 through 1398 to the file, but then the server... actually, the exact interleaving can't be proven from the logs since there's a gap and no migration logging.

What I can prove from the code itself: `refreshChainCaches` seeds `nextSeq` from `max(fileMaxSeq, dbLatestSeq)+1`, so if the file is missing or empty but the database says 1398, the writer starts at 1399 and never backfills. There's no invariant check that the file starts at sequence 1 or that entry count matches `latest_seq`—nothing detects a hole. And `readAllPersistedEntries` only falls back to compressed or legacy formats when the plaintext file is completely empty, so a partially-populated file silently shadows all the fallbacks.

The UI treats a head-truncated stream as a natural conversation start, and the archive gets truncated on non-resume starts. Point 3 is the real culprit for the user-visible loss: the archive fallback exists and would show the full transcript, but the partial file blocks it.

For recovery, I need to rebuild the worker stream file from the archive plus the existing tail in chronological order, renumber it 1 through N, then update `artifact_streams.latest_seq` and `latest_record_id`. The server is live but all three runs are idle, so the risk of concurrent writes is low though not zero. I'll do the repair and then verify it worked. To map archive entries to worker entries, I need to apply the same transformation the system uses. I should lean on the actual code path that handles entry compaction rather than reinventing the logic. The safest approach is to build a dedicated repair script that reads both the archive and current file, merges them in chronological order using the archive as the authoritative source, then renumbers the sequence from 1 onwards.

The script will write atomically using a temp file and rename pattern under the worker lock convention, and update the artifact_streams metadata with the corrected latest_seq and latest_record_id. Since the UI depends on seq ordering for proper merging, renumbering is necessary — and while this is more involved than I'd prefer, it's the bulletproof solution the user needs.

Let me check if there's already an artifact-repair utility in the repo that handles renumbering, so I can reuse existing logic rather than writing from scratch.

--runId <id> or --all-damaged.\");\n    process.exit(1);\n  }\n\n  let repaired = 0;\n  for (const target of targets) {\n    const plan = await planRecovery(target.runId, target.workerId, opts);\n ${repaired} stream(s).` : \"Dry run only — re-run with --apply to write.\");\n}\n\nmain()\n  .then(() => process.exit(0))\n  .catch((error) => {\n    console.error(error);\n    process.exit(1);\n ## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T20:52:49.494Z

I'm going to add a new named event kind for detecting stream head gaps, then create a dedicated healing function that runs in the write path before refreshing the chain caches to handle stranded stream heads with minimal risk.

The healing function will check if the file is empty but the database cursor is advanced, then recover entries from fallback sources like gzip, legacy, or archive storage, renumber them sequentially, write them back to the file, update the database cursor, and invalidate caches — all while holding the file lock to prevent concurrent issues.

Implementing the healing logic...

I'm setting up a regression test that reproduces the exact bug by appending entries, simulating a stream file deletion while keeping the sequence counter advanced, then appending again to verify the transcript recovers the head and maintains integrity.

The challenge is that the test uses the legacy path (no runs row), so the artifact_streams row may not exist—`ensureArtifactStreamRow` would throw and fall back to legacy paths, making `dbLatestSeq` zero and preventing the heal from triggering. To properly test the healing mechanism, I need an artifact_streams row, which requires more setup with the database and a runs row. I'm looking for a test helper that creates a run so I can write a focused, high-value test for the critical invariant using the DB.

## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T20:55:41.321Z

Test 2 is failing because no event gets emitted when it should. The head is recoverable, but after clearing the file, readAllPersistedEntries falls back to checking the archive (which doesn't exist for this test worker) and then the legacy database entries, which returns an empty array. Since there's nothing to recover, it should emit "unrecoverable", but it's not happening.

Looking at the event firing issue — healStrandedStreamHead might be returning early because dbLatestSeq is 0. In test 1, the healing appears to work, but actually the test passes even without recovery: if dbLatestSeq is 0, then nextSeq becomes 1, and the new entry 'd' gets seq 1, which satisfies all the assertions. That's a weak test that masks data loss.

The real problem is that dbLatestSeq stays at 0 because the artifact_streams row either isn't being created or readArtifactStreamMetadata returns nothing. When ensureArtifactStreamRow is called on write, it needs run.projectPath, but the test setup didn't set projectPath on the runs insert, so it's null. This should still create a row though, falling back to app data for the artifact root.

I need to debug whether the row actually exists and check its latest_seq value. More importantly, I should strengthen test 1 to assert that the head entries ('a', 'b', 'c') are actually preserved — that's the real invariant being tested.

  "old_string": "/**\n * Point the DB cursor back at \"empty\" so a fresh file numbers from 1 rather\n * than resuming above a head that no longer exists anywhere.\n */\nasync function resetStreamCursor(runId: string, workerId: string): Promise<void> {\n  try {\n    const { commitArtifactAppend } = await import(\"@/server/artifacts/stream-metadata\");\n    await commitArtifactAppend({\n      streamId: { runId, kind: \"worker_entries\", ownerId: workerId },\n      seq: 0,\n      recordId: \"\",\n    });\n  } catch {\n    // Non-fatal: the append still proceeds, just at the stale cursor.\n  }\n  const key = chainKey(runId, workerId);\n  nextSeqByKey.delete(key);\n  fileStateByKey.delete(key);\n}",
  "new_string": "/**\n * Read the agent runtime's raw output archive for a worker and reassemble it\n * into worker-stream shape.\n *\n * The runtime writes every bridge record here as it streams, so this file\n * outlives stream-file damage. Its records are per-chunk, so streaming deltas\n * must be re-joined (see `reassembleArchivedEntries`) or the transcript comes\n * back shredded mid-word.\n */\nasync function readFromRuntimeOutputArchive(workerId: string): Promise<WorkerEntry[]> {\n  const archivePath = path.join(\n    process.cwd(),\n    \".omniharness\",\n    \"agent-runtime-output\",\n    `${workerId}.jsonl`,\n  );\n  let body: string;\n  try {\n    body = await fs.readFile(archivePath, \"utf8\");\n  } catch {\n    return [];\n  }\n  const parsed = parseWorkerEntryLines(body).filter((entry) => entry.id !== \"output-archive-marker\");\n  if (parsed.length === 0) {\n    return [];\n  }\n  const { reassembleArchivedEntries } = await import(\"@/server/agent-runtime/output-store\");\n  return reassembleArchivedEntries(parsed);\n}\n\n/**\n * Point the DB cursor back at \"empty\" so a fresh file numbers from 1 rather\n * than resuming above a head that no longer exists anywhere.\n *\n * `commitArtifactAppend` deliberately never moves a cursor backward, so this\n * writes the row directly.\n */\nasync function resetStreamCursor(runId: string, workerId: string): Promise<void> {\n  try {\n    const [{ db }, { artifactStreams }, { and, eq: eqOp }] = await Promise.all([\n      import(\"@/server/db\"),\n      import(\"@/server/db/schema\"),\n      import(\"drizzle-orm\"),\n    ]);\n    await db\n      .update(artifactStreams)\n      .set({ latestSeq: 0, latestRecordId: null, updatedAt: new Date() })\n      .where(\n        and(\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.runId, runId),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.kind, \"worker_entries\"),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.ownerId, workerId),\n        ),\n      );\n  } catch {\n    // Non-fatal: the append still proceeds, just at the stale cursor.\n  }\n  const key = chainKey(runId, workerId);\n  nextSeqByKey.delete(key);\n  seenIdsByKey.delete(key);\n  fingerprintsByKey.delete(key);\n  fileStateByKey.delete(key);\n}"
}

  "old_string": "/**\n * Point the DB cursor back at \"empty\" so a fresh file numbers from 1 rather\n * than resuming above a head that no longer exists anywhere.\n *\n * `commitArtifactAppend` deliberately never moves a cursor backward, so this\n * writes the row directly.\n */\nasync function resetStreamCursor(runId: string, workerId: string): Promise<void> {\n  try {\n    const [{ db }, { artifactStreams }, { and, eq: eqOp }] = await Promise.all([\n      import(\"@/server/db\"),\n      import(\"@/server/db/schema\"),\n      import(\"drizzle-orm\"),\n    ]);\n    await db\n      .update(artifactStreams)\n      .set({ latestSeq: 0, latestRecordId: null, updatedAt: new Date() })\n      .where(\n        and(\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.runId, runId),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.kind, \"worker_entries\"),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.ownerId, workerId),\n        ),\n      );\n  } catch {\n    // Non-fatal: the append still proceeds, just at the stale cursor.\n  }\n  const key = chainKey(runId, workerId);\n  nextSeqByKey.delete(key);\n  seenIdsByKey.delete(key);\n  fingerprintsByKey.delete(key);\n  fileStateByKey.delete(key);\n}",
  "new_string": "/**\n * Force `artifact_streams.latest_seq` to match what is actually on disk.\n *\n * `commitArtifactAppend` deliberately never moves a cursor backward, which is\n * right for the append path but wrong for repair — after healing, the file is\n * authoritative and may legitimately be shorter than the stale cursor. This\n * writes the row directly and drops the chain caches so the next write re-reads\n * from the healed file.\n */\nasync function setStreamCursor(\n  runId: string,\n  workerId: string,\n  latestSeq: number,\n  latestRecordId: string | null,\n): Promise<void> {\n  try {\n    const [{ db }, { artifactStreams }, { and: andOp, eq: eqOp }] = await Promise.all([\n      import(\"@/server/db\"),\n      import(\"@/server/db/schema\"),\n      import(\"drizzle-orm\"),\n    ]);\n    await db\n      .update(artifactStreams)\n      .set({ latestSeq, latestRecordId, updatedAt: new Date() })\n      .where(\n        andOp(\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.runId, runId),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.kind, \"worker_entries\"),\n          eqOp(artifactStreams.ownerId, workerId),\n        ),\n      );\n  } catch {\n    // Non-fatal: the append still proceeds, just at the stale cursor.\n  }\n  const key = chainKey(runId, workerId);\n  nextSeqByKey.delete(key);\n  seenIdsByKey.delete(key);\n  fingerprintsByKey.delete(key);\n  fileStateByKey.delete(key);\n}"
}

## Claude · 2026-08-03T21:58:17.523Z

Done. Everything verified: 0 damaged streams remaining, full suite green.

## What actually happened

Two separate faults compounded:

**The trigger** — at 19:33 local, all run-data artifact directories were touched at once. I could *not* prove definitively what did it (the server log has a gap from 19:24–19:40, and the compaction sweep writes nothing to disk). Candidates are a compaction sweep racing the live writer, or a cross-process migration. That part remains unproven.

**The mechanism that turned it into permanent loss** — this I did prove, in code. `refreshChainCaches` seeds the seq cursor as `max(fileMaxSeq, artifact_streams.latest_seq) + 1` (`output-store.ts:767`). When the stream file was missing/empty but the DB cursor already said 1398, the writer resumed numbering at **1399 and never backfilled**. Three things then made it silent and irreversible:

- `readAllPersistedEntries` only consults its fallbacks while the plaintext is *empty* — the moment one entry landed, the partial file shadowed them forever.
- Its "archive" fallback reads the run `.zip`, **not** the runtime jsonl that actually held your data. So auto-recovery was never possible.
- `readWorkerEntriesBefore` returns `hasOlder: false` at the truncation point, so the UI rendered it as a natural conversation start.

You were not the only casualty: **five** streams were damaged, the oldest from **June 14** — this bug had been quietly eating transcripts for seven weeks.

## Recovery

All five restored from the runtime archives, verified contiguous and chronological:

| run | before | after | span |
|---|---|---|---|
| **e51514929b72** | 358 (seq 1399+) | **1273** | 16:58:54 → 17:37:27 |
| e74cf7a81b7f | 471 (seq 268+) | 369 | full |
| ef23fac96fdb | 195 (seq 773+) | 669 | full |
| 1795ba24270e | 42 (seq 1278+) | 1193 | full |
| ab01d86e943c | 338 | 338 (cursor fixed) | full |

Your messages are back at seq 1 and seq 179 (17:02:39), where you actually sent them.

**On the shredded text you caught** — that was my bug, and a real one. The archive stores *streaming deltas* (178 fragments like `'I'`, `"'ll investigate..."`), while the stream stores assembled messages. I replayed fragments verbatim. The fix follows `appendMessageChunk`: same-type `message`/`thought` chunks rejoin, any other record ends the run. I validated it against the surviving tail — all 12 message and 14 thought bodies reproduce **byte-for-byte**. Good catch; I'd have shipped that.

## Prevention

- **`healStrandedStreamHead`** — before any append, if the file is empty while the cursor is advanced, recover the head and renumber from 1 rather than resuming mid-stream. One `stat` on the hot path.
- **Runtime archive wired into recovery** — the source that saved you is now reachable automatically, with delta reassembly.
- **Archives rotate instead of delete** — `truncate: !resume` was destroying the only escape hatch on every non-resume start. Now keeps 3 rotations.
- **Loud failure** — `worker.stream_head_healed` / `worker.stream_head_unrecoverable` events; silent truncation is no longer possible.
- **`scripts/recover-worker-transcript.ts`** — doubles as an audit (`--all-damaged`, dry-run by default).

Files changed: `src/server/workers/output-store.ts`, `src/server/agent-runtime/output-store.ts`, `src/server/events/named-events.ts`, plus the new script and test.

**Verification:** 2440 tests pass (375 files), typecheck clean, lint clean. Three regression tests reproduce the exact failure — I confirmed they fail against the old code first; the first version passed for the wrong reason and I had to fix it.

Backups are read-only at `~/omniharness-transcript-rescue-20260803/` (4 archives + original run-data). Per-file `.pre-recovery-*.bak` sit beside each rewritten stream. Nothing is committed — the working tree already had unrelated changes, so I left staging to you.

One caveat worth flagging: the recovered transcripts are rebuilt from the raw archive, so entry *ids and seq numbers differ* from the originals. Content and ordering are faithful; the identifiers are not the same ones the client cached. A hard refresh is the clean way to view them.

So the cache key is `omni-worker-entries-cache:v1`, and the stale fragments are persisting because my initial recovery pass created around 1900 fragment entries with IDs that got cached in the browser. The frontend coalesces entries by ID and merges the cached data with server responses, so those old fragment IDs like "a2" are still rendering even though they no longer exist on the server.

The immediate fix for the user is to clear both cache keys from localStorage and reload. But the better systemic solution is to bump the cache version from `:v1` to `:v2` — since my repaired data has completely different entry IDs than the shredded pass, any client with the old cache is now inconsistent. Incrementing the version invalidates all stale caches automatically and prevents anyone from seeing the corrupted data.

Since the repair changed entry ids, every existing client cache is now stale. Bumping the version invalidates them all automatically.
